review: Drafted by Claude for the purpose; no label has had human review yet. The same author wrote the labels and the candidate checks, so the held-out test split guards against tuning, not against the author's blind spots.
description: Labelled (topic, question) pairs for AI-10's question-relevance check (after generation). Every question is a four-option MCQ that passes the support and exam checks against the page it cites, so each off-topic pair is supported by its passage but not about the requested topic.
labelling_rule: on_topic: topics (all covered) the question is about; off_topic: topics it is not about, chosen from the same document, a same-course near miss and an out-of-corpus subject. A pair never mixes splits.

item.prompt: When do we write lim(x→a) f(x) = L?

options.text: When f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x sufficiently close to a
When f is defined at a

item.explanation: The limit is L when f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close to a, but not equal to a.

item.prompt: For f(x) = |x|/x, what is the right-hand limit at 0?
item.explanation: For f(x) = |x|/x the right-hand limit at 0 is 1 and the left-hand limit is −1.

item.prompt: What is lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2)?
item.explanation: Factorise and cancel: lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = lim(x→2) (x + 2) = 4.

item.prompt: Which theorem proves that lim(x→0) x² sin(1/x) = 0?
item.explanation: The squeeze theorem is how we prove that lim(x→0) x² sin(1/x) = 0.

item.prompt: What is lim(x→∞) (3x² + 1)/(2x² − 5)?
item.explanation: If the degrees are equal, the limit as x→∞ is the ratio of the leading coefficients: 3/2.

item.prompt: Which condition is required for f to be continuous at a?

options.text: The limit of f at a exists and equals f(a)
f has a jump at a

item.explanation: A function f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a).

item.prompt: What is a removable discontinuity?

options.text: A hole that can be filled by redefining one value
A jump with unequal one-sided limits

item.explanation: A removable discontinuity is a hole that can be filled by redefining one value.

item.prompt: Which theorem is used to show that an equation has a root in an interval?
item.explanation: The Intermediate Value Theorem is often used to show that an equation has a root in an interval.

item.prompt: Which limit defines the derivative of f at x from first principles?
item.explanation: The derivative of f at x is f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h.

item.prompt: Why does |x| have no derivative at 0?

options.text: It is continuous at 0 but has a corner there

item.explanation: |x| is continuous at 0 yet has a corner, so it has no derivative at 0.

item.prompt: Using the product rule, what is d/dx (eˣ sin x)?

options.text: eˣ sin x + eˣ cos x
eˣ sin x − eˣ cos x

item.explanation: By the product rule, d/dx (eˣ sin x) = eˣ sin x + eˣ cos x.

item.prompt: Where is the quotient rule (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g² valid?
item.explanation: The quotient rule (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g² is valid wherever g ≠ 0.

item.prompt: Using the chain rule, what is d/dx (sin 3x)?
item.explanation: By the chain rule, differentiate the outside function, keep the inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside: d/dx (sin 3x) = 3 cos 3x.

item.prompt: According to the power rule, what is d/dx (xⁿ)?
item.explanation: Power rule: d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹ for any real n.

item.prompt: If y is defined implicitly by x² + y² = 25, what is dy/dx?
item.explanation: From x² + y² = 25 we get 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.

item.prompt: If f″(x) > 0 at a stationary point, what is the point?
item.explanation: The second derivative test classifies stationary points: if f″(x) > 0 the point is a local minimum.

item.prompt: A spherical balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s. Which expression gives dV/dt?
item.explanation: Its volume V = (4/3)πr³ changes at dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt.

item.prompt: What happens between like charges?
item.explanation: Charge comes in two kinds; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

item.prompt: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, why does the rod become positively charged?

options.text: Protons move from the silk to the glass
Electrons move from the silk to the glass
Electrons move from the glass to the silk

item.explanation: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, electrons move from the glass to the silk, leaving the rod positively charged.

item.prompt: In Millikan's oil-drop experiment, what was balanced against the electric force?

options.text: The weight of tiny charged oil drops
The magnetic force on the drops

item.explanation: Robert Millikan measured e by balancing the weight of tiny charged oil drops against an electric force.

item.prompt: Under Coulomb's law, what happens to the force between two point charges when their separation is doubled?
item.explanation: Because of the inverse-square dependence F = k q₁q₂ / r², doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter of its value.

item.prompt: Why does copper conduct electricity well?

options.text: Its electrons are bound to their atoms
Its outer electrons are free to move through the material

item.explanation: In a conductor such as copper, outer electrons are free to move through the material.

item.prompt: What is the electric field at a point?

options.text: The rate of flow of charge
The force per unit positive test charge
The work done per unit charge

item.explanation: The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q, measured in N/C.

item.prompt: Where are electric field lines closer together?
item.explanation: Field lines never cross, and they are closer together where the field is stronger.

item.prompt: What is the electric potential V at a point?

options.text: The work done per unit charge in bringing a positive test charge from infinity to the point
The force per unit charge at the point
The rate of flow of charge

item.explanation: The electric potential V is the work done per unit charge in bringing a positive test charge from infinity to the point.

item.prompt: What does Ohm's law state for a metallic conductor at constant temperature?

options.text: The current is proportional to the potential difference across it
The current is proportional to its resistance

item.explanation: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, the current through a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR.

item.prompt: In R = ρL/A, what is ρ?
item.explanation: R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity, L the length and A the cross-sectional area.

item.prompt: How does the combined resistance of resistors in parallel compare with the smallest single resistor?

options.text: It is smaller than the smallest single resistor
It is larger than the largest resistor

item.explanation: Resistors in parallel satisfy 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, so the total is smaller than the smallest single resistor.

item.prompt: Kirchhoff's voltage law expresses the conservation of what?
item.explanation: Kirchhoff's voltage law: around any closed loop the sum of the potential differences is zero, which expresses conservation of energy.

item.prompt: A kettle is rated 2000 W on a 230 V supply. About what current does it draw?
item.explanation: Electrical power is P = VI, so a kettle rated 2000 W on a 230 V supply draws a current of about 8.7 A.

item.prompt: What is electric current?

options.text: The work done per unit charge
The rate of flow of charge

item.explanation: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, measured in amperes.

item.prompt: What is the sign of ΔH for an exothermic reaction?

options.text: It depends on the temperature only

item.explanation: An exothermic reaction releases heat to its surroundings, so its enthalpy change ΔH is negative.

item.prompt: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state?
item.explanation: By definition ΔHf° of an element in its standard state is zero.

item.prompt: What does Hess's law state about the total enthalpy change of a reaction?

options.text: It depends on the route taken
It equals the bond enthalpies of the products
It is the same whichever route is taken from reactants to products

item.explanation: Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whichever route is taken, as long as the initial and final states are the same.

item.prompt: In a calorimeter, which expression gives the heat absorbed by water?
item.explanation: In a calorimeter, the heat absorbed by water is q = mcΔT.

item.prompt: How do bond enthalpies estimate ΔH?

options.text: The enthalpy of formation of the elements
Energy to break bonds minus energy released forming bonds
Energy released forming bonds plus energy to break bonds

item.explanation: Bond enthalpies give an estimate: ΔH ≈ (energy to break bonds) − (energy released forming bonds).

item.prompt: Hess's law lets us calculate which enthalpy changes?

options.text: Enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly
Only changes measured in a calorimeter

item.explanation: Hess's law lets us calculate enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly by combining equations whose ΔH values are known.

item.prompt: Where does a prokaryotic cell keep its DNA?

options.text: In a region called the nucleoid

item.explanation: Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, have no nucleus; their DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid.

item.prompt: What is the mitochondrion the site of?
item.explanation: The mitochondrion is the site of aerobic respiration, where glucose is oxidised to release energy stored as ATP.

item.prompt: Which structures do plant cells have in addition to animal cell organelles?

options.text: Chloroplasts, a cellulose cell wall and a large permanent vacuole

item.explanation: Plant cells also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis, a cellulose cell wall and a large permanent vacuole.

item.prompt: What is the structure of the cell membrane?

options.text: A phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it

item.explanation: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it; it is selectively permeable.

item.prompt: Does diffusion need energy from the cell?

options.text: No, diffusion needs no energy from the cell

item.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration; it needs no energy from the cell.

item.prompt: What happens to a plant cell placed in pure water?

options.text: It takes in water and becomes turgid
It loses water and becomes plasmolysed

item.explanation: Osmosis moves water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one: a plant cell placed in pure water takes in water and becomes turgid.

item.prompt: Which process lets root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil against a concentration gradient?
item.explanation: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient and uses energy from ATP, as when root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil.

item.prompt: What happens to a plant cell placed in a concentrated salt solution?

options.text: It loses water and becomes plasmolysed
It takes in water and becomes turgid

item.explanation: In a concentrated salt solution a plant cell loses water and becomes plasmolysed.

item.prompt: Which list method adds one item at the end of a list?
item.explanation: Because lists are mutable you can change them in place: append adds one item at the end.

item.prompt: How are tuples written in Python?
item.explanation: Tuples are written with round brackets, such as (3, 1, 2), and are often used for fixed records like coordinates.

item.prompt: What happens when an operation seems to modify a string?

options.text: It actually builds a new string
It changes the string in place
It converts the string to a list

item.explanation: Strings are immutable: once created they cannot be changed, so an operation that seems to modify a string actually builds a new one.

item.prompt: What does s[1:3] return for a sequence s?
item.explanation: Slicing: s[1:3] returns the items at positions 1 and 2.

item.prompt: Which values can be dictionary keys?

options.text: Immutable values such as strings, numbers or tuples

item.explanation: A dictionary maps keys to values; keys must be immutable, such as strings, numbers or tuples.

item.prompt: What is a quick way to remove repeated values from a list?

options.text: Convert the list to a tuple
Converting the list to a set

item.explanation: A set is an unordered collection with no duplicates; converting a list to a set is a quick way to remove repeated values.

item.prompt: What does [x * x for x in range(5)] give?
item.explanation: A list comprehension builds a list in one expression: [x * x for x in range(5)] gives [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].

item.prompt: Why is looking up a dictionary key fast on average regardless of its size?

options.text: Keys are stored in a list
Dictionaries are implemented as hash tables

item.explanation: Looking up a key is fast on average regardless of the dictionary's size, because dictionaries are implemented as hash tables.

item.prompt: What is the mode of a data set?

options.text: The value that occurs most often
The sum divided by the count

item.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often, and a data set can have more than one mode.

item.prompt: For the scores 45, 50, 55, 60 and 290, what are the mean and the median?
item.explanation: The mean is sensitive to outliers: for the scores 45, 50, 55, 60 and 290, the mean is 100 but the median is 55.

item.prompt: For a sample, what is the sum of squared deviations divided by to give the variance?
item.explanation: The variance is the average squared deviation from the mean; for a sample we divide the sum of squared deviations by n − 1.

item.prompt: What does the interquartile range measure?

options.text: The largest value minus the smallest
The spread of the middle half of the data

item.explanation: The interquartile range, Q3 − Q1, measures the spread of the middle half of the data and resists outliers.

item.prompt: Which is an example of unstructured data?

options.text: Rows and columns of a fixed format

item.explanation: Unstructured data has no predefined model; examples are emails, photographs, audio recordings and free-text survey answers.

item.prompt: Which is an example of qualitative data?

options.text: Number of students in a class

item.explanation: Qualitative data describes categories, such as department or blood group; quantitative data is numerical.

item.prompt: When is quantitative data discrete?
item.explanation: Quantitative data is discrete when it is counted, such as the number of students in a class, and continuous when it is measured.

item.prompt: What is the range of a data set?

options.text: The largest value minus the smallest
The square root of the variance

item.explanation: The range is the largest value minus the smallest.

item.prompt: For an even number of values, how is the median found?

options.text: The sum of the values divided by the count
The average of the two middle values
The larger of the two middle values

item.explanation: The median is the middle value when the data are sorted; for an even number of values it is the average of the two middle values.
